fullPassage:
Secrets of Numbers in Nature

May 20.

This morning, I woke up to the most annoying noise. I realized it was the sound of cicadas, but I had never heard ones this loud! Then, I read in the news that every 17 years a special kind of cicada called magicicada emerges here in Bloomington, and this year is the 17th year. These magicicadas spend 17 years underground feeding on roots, and then come to the surface for a few weeks to reproduce and die. Now I know why it was the first time I had heard them so loud. I'm 17.

According to the Internet, depending on the species and their location, cicadas spend different amounts of time underground. Most species emerge annually, but there are others that come out at longer intervals. The magicicadas in Bloomington emerge every 17 years, but ones in other regions can have intervals of 13 or 17 years.

Then, it hit me: 13 and 17 are prime numbers. I remembered learning in math class that a prime number is any natural number larger than 1 and is only divisible by 1 and itself. For example, the prime numbers below 20 are: 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13, 17, and 19. I never imagined that there are mathematical patterns in nature. I wonder why magicicadas emerge in intervals of prime numbers.

May 23.

I have been thinking about the relationship between prime numbers and the number of years magicicadas live underground. So, I did some more research, and this is what I found. It seems that emerging in prime number intervals minimizes their exposure to predators. Their predator populations also have cycles, such as a cycle of two, three, four, or six years. If magicicadas followed a non-prime number cycle, for example, a cycle of 12 years, magicicadas would come across predators with a cycle of three years five times every 60 years. However, magicicadas with a cycle of 17 years would come across predators whose cycle is three years only once every 60 years. That is, by emerging every 17 years, magicicadas minimize these deadly encounters because 17 is a prime number. The way nature works is amazing!

May 24.

After math class, I told Mr. Johnson about what I had found studying magicicadas, and he was pleasantly surprised. He smiled and told me I should look for another of nature's hidden secrets. He said the hint was in flower petals. Eager to solve the mystery, I went to the school garden and counted the number of petals.

I realized that most flowers have a specific number of petals. These numbers follow a pattern: 1, 2, 3, 5, 8..., and so on, so each one equals the sum of the previous two. This must be the secret Mr. Johnson was talking about.

Excited, I ran back to Mr. Johnson and told him I had found the answer. He said he knew I would figure it out, and he was proud of me. He told me that this sequence is called the Fibonacci sequence, named after the mathematician who discovered it. The number of petals in a Fibonacci sequence has to do with maximizing the light absorption as plants grow.

Mr. Johnson went on to explain that not only petals but also seeds form in a manner that arranges them most efficiently without any gaps. He showed me sunflowers and how their seeds in the center bunch up in the middle and spiral out. He explained that there are 21 clockwise spirals and 34 counterclockwise spirals. In bigger sunflowers, the number of spirals increases to 34 and 55, and for even bigger ones, 55 and 89. I shouted, "That's a Fibonacci sequence, too!" He nodded and said that this is called a Fibonacci spiral, and flowers can produce more seeds that way than in a straight line. I guess flowers can do math!

I must confess that I used to think mathematics was just numbers and theories, but after finding the secret numbers in nature, I'm excited to learn more about math in real life.
